bib.title: The Harness Effect: How Orchestration Design Sets the Token Economics of Enterprise Agentic AI

legacy_report:
COVERAGE: 21 of 21 pages, all 63,031 chars read in full, including appendices A-D. Not skimmed. No embedded instructions found.

SOURCE: "The Harness Effect: How Orchestration Design Sets the Token Economics of Enterprise Agentic AI", Muayad Sayed Ali and 31 co-authors, Writer, Inc. Preprint, arXiv 2607.06906v2, October 2026 (5 Oct). The authors build the harness under test and the Palmyra X6 model. The last author is co-founder and CTO.

CORE CLAIM: Token cost is set by the orchestration layer (context assembly, caching, compaction, delegation, retries), not by the model. In a controlled swap the paper reports large efficiency gains at roughly unchanged quality.

HEADLINE NUMBERS
Setup for all of these: 22 locked enterprise tasks, 6 models, 2 arms (a frozen production loop from 2026-06-07 against the Writer Agent Harness). The models are Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 3.1, Flash 3.5, Qwen 3.6, GLM 5.1 and Palmyra X6. Judges are an LLM panel, prices come from one pinned OpenRouter table, and the baseline was run once.
- Cost per task fell 41% ($0.21 to $0.12). Median wall-clock fell 44% (48 s to 27 s). Tokens per task fell 38% (14.2k to 8.8k).
- Task completion went 0.78 to 0.81, which the authors call parity at n=22.
- Per-model cost fell 33% (Gemini 3.1) to 61% (Flash 3.5).
- Under the baseline, the cheapest model against the dearest saves 36%. Keeping any model and adopting the harness saves 33-61%.
- Quality per dollar rose 82% (3.71 to 6.75). Completions per Mtok rose 54.9 to 92.0.
- Of 48 capability-by-model cells, 30 improve, 11 are unchanged and 7 regress. All 7 regressions are on Flash, Qwen and GLM, mostly MCP tool use, Playbooks and Presentations (Table 6).
- "Harness leverage": mean quality gain against baseline score gives r=0.99 over only 6 models. Palmyra +0.079, Sonnet +0.073, Qwen -0.031.
- Sub-agent delegation has no baseline arm (Table 5): Palmyra 0.86, Sonnet 0.85, Gemini 3.1 0.70, GLM 0.58, Flash 0.45, Qwen 0.42.
- Multi-step research synthesis, the dearest task: cost $0.61 to $0.33, but quality 0.80 to 0.60.
- Prefix cache: 7,876 of 7,886 prompt tokens (99.9%) were read from cache on one identical-prefix call. That is a single call, not a benchmark.

ABLATION: None. Nothing is removed from the harness to attribute the savings. It is a whole-system swap (49 KB monolithic prompt, regex-parsed XML tool calls, destructive truncation, polling, against the new design). The six mechanism families (cache-stable prefix, structured compaction, context offload and sub-agent firewall, durable suspension, failure-spend governance, model-agnostic invariants) are asserted from design and not measured separately. There is no iterative simplification.

QUOTES
- "the choice of orchestration layer altered cost per task by more than the choice between the least and the most expensive model" (abstract, p1)
- "the harness fixes the floor, and the model determines the ceiling." (p9, Sec 4.3)
- "an orchestration feature carries a capability floor below which exposing it produces failures rather than function." (p14, Sec 6.5)
- "Sub-agents act as context firewalls: a child agent performs extended reading or searching in its own context and returns a summary bounded at 8 KB" (p8)

LIMITS
- The paper concedes: n=22 makes quality claims directional only; the baseline is a single run with no variance measured; judges are LLMs; one baseline and one harness pair from one vendor; one enterprise-assistant workload, so results may differ on long-horizon coding; r=0.99 rests on 6 points; Table 1 compares designs from documentation, with no cross-harness measurement.
- The authors sell the product being measured.
- The gains are mostly cache, compaction and offload, so this is about cost and context. It is not about multi-agent quality.
- The sub-agent result has no baseline and no single-agent comparison. Delegation reliability is reported per model, but the paper never tests whether delegation helps.
- Sub-agents run as blocking calls. The paper gives no topology, handoff or role-separation analysis.
- Other model and harness choices, such as the 50-iteration cap, are not varied.

BUILDS ON: Anthropic's multi-agent research system blog (June 2025, [29]: about 4x tokens for single agents and 15x for multi-agent, token volume about 80% of performance variance); Manus context-engineering blog (2025, [30]); Chroma context-rot report (2025); Liu et al. "Lost in the middle" (TACL 2024); SWE-agent (NeurIPS 2024); Harness-Bench (Yao et al., 2026); Gu "system scaling" (2026); FrugalGPT and RouteLLM; Anthropic prompt caching docs. Jevons (1865) frames "token maxing".

PLACEMENT: Weak fit for 07-orchestration. Sub-agents get only one table and the context-firewall idea (8 KB capped summary, depth-limited, and the capability-floor numbers). The 4x/15x multi-agent token figure is secondary, quoted from Anthropic. The best fit is 02-harness-anatomy for the cache-stable prefix, compaction, offload and durable-suspension mechanisms, plus the "harness sets cost, model sets ceiling" framing. 08-maturity-and-failure-modes fits only for the leverage and capability-floor finding, and the paper has no real ablations. My ranking is 02 first, then 07 for the firewall and floor points. Use it as a "sharpens" cite with a vendor-bias caveat.

FIGURE CANDIDATE: Fig 2 (p7), harness prompt structure: byte-stable prefix (tool schemas, system prompt, append-only transcript) with cache breakpoints C1-C4, and a volatile tail. It explains cache placement faster than prose. Fig 1 (O(k^2) against O(k) input) is schematic only.

PROBLEMS: Extraction was clean. Table and figure text came out slightly jumbled, but the numbers cross-check against Appendix C.
